newsitem.title: USA: Japan monetary policy aims to ensure recovery-BOJ.
newsitem.headline: Japan monetary policy aims to ensure recovery-BOJ.

text.p: Japan's monetary policy will aim to secure a basis for economic recovery while keeping close watch over monetary and economic conditions, Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita said Saturday.

"Japan's economy is continuing gradual growth ... Our monetary policy will emphasize putting the basis for current economic recovery on firmer ground while keeping close watch over monetary and economic conditions," Matsushita said at a news conference at the conclusion of G7 talks today.
Of economic conditions in other G7 nations, Matsushita said the U.S. economy was growing strongly amid stable prices while the European economy showed signs it was picking up.
In a report, the IMF also said that the global economy is likely to expand next year without much inflationary fear.
Matsushita said global macroeconomic conditions were looking good.

On Japan's financial system, he said banks were steadily coping with problem loans. He said he explained to the G7 nations that the government was implementing new schemes to cope with financial failures.
"Both the private and public sectors will make efforts to regain credibility (in the Japanese financial system) both at home and abroad," Matsushita said.
Japanese Finance Minister Wataru Kubo told the same news conference that he told G7 nations that Japan's economy was continuing to recover, but that he also urged the need for fiscal consolidation.
However, none of the G7 nations asked Japan to take additional monetary or fiscal steps to boost its economy.
"There was no mention made. Even though our economic policy is related to global issues, it is up to us to decide on the current monetary and fiscal policies," Kubo said.
Matsushita also said European countries face the need to tackle structural reforms to cope with high unemployment and fiscal deficits.

Asked whether the weaker yen would help Japanese exporters gain competitiveness and thus slow down the pace of decline in Japan's trade surplus, Kubo said, "The current account surplus is continuing to shrink steadily. I think this trend will continue."
Kubo said the yen's declining trend has continued for the past three years and said the key for a stronger economic recovery was recovery in private sector demand.
The stronger recovery in the economy will make it possible to lighten fiscal support, he said.
"The strength of the recovery can be judged by the extent of self-sustainable recovery in private sector demand. By strengthening the economy, we can lighten support from the government," Kubo said.
"We can find a way to achieve economic recovery and fiscal consolidation," he said.
